What a continuum's parts cannot differ in is their essence as parts of a continuous whole. They can still differ in their individual identities and positions in the whole.

The objector's argument reverses the point. “Finite” here means having a limit in the sense of a boundary, not the opposite of infinity as a number. The past has a boundary on the side that reaches us, but that does not make it finite without qualification. Existence is not a container that counts and confines all that enters it; an infinite series can exist, and there can be more than one infinite series.

Suppose a body has existed forever and has always undergone events with no first event, such as a heavenly sphere passing through an endless series of positions. On the argument being examined, the body cannot be earlier than the whole series of events, since there is no first one. Nor can it be earlier than their absence, since that absence is also said to be eternal. Some manuscripts repeat the words 'and is earlier' at this point.

A contradiction then threatens. The body is not earlier than the events, by the assumption just made. Yet it also seems that it is earlier: it exists together with the supposed eternal absence of the events, and what exists with something earlier should itself be earlier. Or the body is earlier than every particular event; the whole series has no existence beyond those particular events, so it should be earlier than the series too.

Another problem appears. The body is said not to precede the events, yet it must precede the eternal absence that is earlier than each event. Whatever has truly existed eternally cannot at the same time have been absent; the supposed eternal absence comes to an end when an event begins. This is another way to state the difficulty.

The reasoning may also be put like this: although the body is not prior to the collection of events considered together, it is prior to each event. Since the collection has no separate existence apart from its members, that difference is hard to maintain. The same point will become clearer in the reply to the eighth objection, where something that always accompanies changing events is said to precede their individual occurrences.

The wording needs care. 'Of these things' may explain what is meant by 'each one.' The repeated phrase in some copies is probably a copying error. The final claim that such priority is impossible may be intended to support the denial that the body precedes the eternal absence: if the body does not precede the events that come after that absence, how could it precede the absence itself?

The first argument resembles the proof that spatial dimensions are finite: compare the number of past cycles, years, or souls with the same number plus one from the future. The comparison assumes that all these things can be gathered together. But past events do not coexist as one collection; only the imagination gathers them. Bodily powers are finite, and the intellect, which is immaterial, cannot be measured by this comparison.

The first part of the argument repeats the second: if prior nonexistence is in time, it already assumes the conclusion. The other reading—that an earlier existence entails later nonexistence—is the converse of the same point.

A better argument would say that the whole collection begins because each event in it begins. But the whole has no existence separate from its members. This is not always a fallacy: it works for a connected continuum, where the whole and its parts are connected. Sadra himself argues that every bodily event is renewed and surrounded by nonexistence, and therefore the whole natural world is renewed too. Without this point, that conclusion would be unsupported.
Most philosophers say that the collection exists as one whole. Sadra denies that it has a separate existence of its own.

At every moment there is a new collection of departed rational souls, as more people die and leave their bodies. The world as a whole is also renewed continually. This may refer to substantial motion, as Sadra holds, or to the idea that the whole world changes because some of its parts pass away at every moment. The first reading better fits his account; the second fits the immediate example.

That is, the event cannot be described as having no beginning. Yet an endless series of events need have neither a last event nor a first event. There was no particular time empty of events: to say that something is beginningless is, in this use, to deny a first moment, not to name a time. This answer is closest to the opponent’s own way of thinking.

A stronger answer distinguishes the senses in which we speak of eternity. Sometimes we mean the indefinitely distant past. That is still time: a continuous extent whose parts pass away. It would be unworthy of God to say that His existence, attributes or action belong to such a past. Sometimes we mean something like the setting for an existence beyond all completeness, from which the descending order of beings begins. What corresponds to it at the end of the ascending order is called everlastingness. Both belong to the order flowing from God. In a still fuller sense, eternity refers to existence before all particular forms and limitations, without viewing it merely as the beginning of beginnings or the end of ends. True oneness sets aside these relations.

In the last two senses, eternity is no bounded time. It embraces all such settings of existence, including past and future times, as necessary existence encompasses the essences of things. Scripture and those who speak on God’s behalf use it in these senses when referring to His existence, attributes, and power to act. The same distinctions apply to everlastingness.

The objector's argument about the possibility of events is meant to imply that God's power must have a beginning. For theologians, the possibility of the world and its being created are tied to divine power. The commentator says this makes the objection too long and weak: possibility belongs to the created world, while power belongs to God. A sharper reply is that possibility is the same as potentiality, and it cannot itself have a beginning.

The objector means that existence has bounded past events on the side that reaches the present. The reply is that this does not prove a beginning on the other side. The argument can also be turned against the claim that events can begin.

The seventh argument may mean that the body is described both by all past events and by their nonexistence, which would be contradictory. But the whole collection of past events does not exist at once. Or it may mean that the body is described at each moment by one event and by the absence of another. That is not contradictory: the event present at that time is not the event absent from it.

This notes a hidden individual case, as opposed to the obvious case of any one event. If “the world” is a collection, each moment has a new collection of events; if it means every individual event, none of those individuals is absent from the world as a whole in the same sense.
This objection answers those who define “the world” as everything other than God, and who accept separate intellects. It does not apply to those who mean only the bodily world by “the world.”
This wording points toward Sadra's own argument: if the world had not begun, it would precede and be separate from its events, contrary to what is assumed.

The point is that a subject that never lacks events would, if those events were finite, have to precede the earliest event. If the events are infinite, however, any event the subject precedes is itself preceded by another event, and so on without end.

Sadra accepts the eighth argument, but gives it a different meaning. The world is always accompanied by changing events, and what is never without change has itself begun in time. This means that each bodily substance, nature, soul, and accident is preceded by temporal nonexistence; it does not mean that there was one first time after which the world began all at once.
“What is in the mind” means the existence of the world as represented in the mind—in other words, the world as known by someone who knows it.

This anticipates the conclusion: the opponent's position would make the world's existence depend on something other than God. It also does not follow that the world's actual existence is finite; the past may be an endless succession, though not one collection that exists all at once.

The “whole collection” is either an imagined collection of events or a collection that exists outside the mind. If it is imagined, it began as a mental picture. If it is taken to exist in the world, it is finite because past events no longer exist and future ones do not yet exist; the infinite series is successive, not one whole.

The past-tense word “was” implies both existence and time. If it means only “was nonexistent, then came to exist,” the claim still assumes succession and contradicts the view that time itself belongs to the world.
Priority in the order of nature is essential: a possible thing is nothing by itself and exists only through its cause. What belongs to a thing by itself is prior to what it has through another.

The same issue appears in Jamal al-Din al-Khwansari's claim that the religious view requires a gap between God and the world. This would make God's existence new or limited, and would place pure, all-encompassing existence alongside the world.
The philosophers say priority has several degrees, and causal priority is the clearest and most deserving of being called priority.

The parties may also disagree about whether God's giving is unending and His words never pass away, while what receives existence is temporary and limited. One side says that what belongs to God is eternal and what comes from Him is new; the other reverses this. Then the difference between belief in a creator and denying one becomes clear. It also distinguishes belief in God's oneness from imagining Him as a body: power, when treated as a bodily capacity, depends on matter. The note connects this issue to the Qur'anic image of God's hands being tied, and argues that the best account of creation preserves both God's perfect names and attributes and the world's renewal.

This can mean, first, that denying God's oneness in action makes Him one among several agents: some new event or will would share the work of bringing the world into being. That added agent would itself have to be necessary in existence, or the world would not be new. Second, the phrase can mean that denying oneness in what is produced does not imply that God's own essence is multiple; philosophers hold that one source gives rise to one thing.

A second agent would also conflict with God's will being one in its relation to all things, His knowledge being active, His will effective, and His existence necessary in every respect. It would also make Him seem to withhold the goodness and generosity that follow from wisdom and fullness, or to fall silent instead of endlessly speaking and giving.

The mystic's criticism assumes that “the world is eternal in time” means that the world has existed only since time existed. If “world” means everything other than God, the phrase may be using “time” broadly to include the everlasting age; if it means pure intellects, “with time” can mean that they coexist with their cause. In either case, it need not mean that all things are measured by ordinary time.
The idea that time existed before bodies is a weak interpretation and has no place in a serious account.
The Persian couplet means: “Where You are, there is no me; / no one can enter this mystery.” The point is that beings are related to God, while God is not dependent on them.

The mystic's words do not prove that the world began. Those who say that the heavens and basic elements last forever can accept that God is beyond time and that effects do not exist in the same way as their cause.

A bodily power is limited both in its own capacity and in what it can do or undergo. Since it is spread through a body, its strength changes with the body's size and cannot exceed the body's limits. The note says the question of its power to act and be affected will be discussed later.

This is the first of two ways to understand the opponent's reply. The world, as one individual existence, may have only limited power and may not last forever by itself, yet its effects may be continually supplied by a higher source. The note reads this as a view that denies substantial motion and treats the world's existence as numerically fixed.
This answer rules out the first interpretation, so the text can turn to the second.
This is the flowing now, which traces or produces time as it flows, just as motion through the middle of a path traces the motion considered as a whole.

Cutting time apart would also cut the celestial motion that measures it, and that would make the celestial body stop. The note also says that cutting time in principle means a break in the flow of existence.

“In time” is broader than “at the boundary of time.” Something that occurs at an instant is still temporal, since an instant is the boundary of time. So instantaneous things and things spread across time can both be called temporal.
For example, contact that lasts for a while.
For example, reaching a point along a path while moving.

A fuller account of where things exist distinguishes the eternal realm, where God exists; higher and lower levels of the timeless realm, where intellects and universal souls exist; higher and lower levels of the realm of suspended forms and universal natural principles; existence in an instant; and two ways of existing in time—with something spread across it or without being spread across it. The book gives examples of these kinds.

You might object that if something can occur in an instant, it must exist only in an instant. Here, however, “now” means the flowing now, which produces time rather than contradicting it. The author later says that a moving thing is never without motion or rest at any instant of its motion. Motion itself cannot occur in a single instant, and rest is not actual motion. Yet at each instant the moving thing is still described as moving. Not having a specific kind of motion does not mean it has no motion at all.
The first either-or asks whether a thing occurs all at once or not all at once. The second asks whether its coming to be has a first instant or has none. These are not the same question.

“Gradually” here means strictly spread across time, not the broader sense of moving from potential to actual. That broader meaning also includes motion through the middle of a path, which exists in time without matching it part for part.

The phrase “and it does not exist at the start of that time” means that it is not present at the first instant, which would make it instantaneous. Something spread across time has an extension and parts corresponding to parts of time. Something that exists in time without being spread across it has no parts or extension; motion through the middle of a path is simple but flowing, as are the absence of an instant and other cases discussed later. The first kind is present throughout its time; the second occurs in time without extending across it.

Avicenna's wording in The Healing is: “It is proper to ask whether the shared instant between two stretches of time can be free of both states, or whether one state must be present there.” In the present text, some words needed to introduce the question seem to be missing. Perhaps the author is shortening Avicenna's passage, or using “whether” as in the question “Does it exist?”

You might say that motion begins at the shared instant, so there are not two instants. The reply is that the shared instant belongs to rest; the moving thing has not yet begun moving. Its first instant of motion must come after the shared instant.

Motion through the middle of a path is simple but not at rest, so it cannot exist at a single fixed instant. The flowing now is what suits it. As Avicenna says, it is a renewed state of the moving thing, a changing nearness or distance. Since its state is never the same, Plato called motion “a departure from equality.”
For example, an angle formed as one line moves alongside another, discussed later.

For example, the contact of a moving cone with a stationary cone at their tips. Their contact occurs in an instant, but its absence unfolds through time without matching time part for part. The same is true when one sphere moves away from another after they touch.

One might say that absence of contact is temporal, not instantaneous, so this does not divide the contact itself. The answer is that “gradual” here has the strict meaning of being spread across time. It does not mean every kind of change from potential to actual, which includes both motion through the middle of a path and motion considered as a whole. Strictly speaking, motion through the middle is the real gradual process.
That is, an interval of time between the two instants. The word “between” makes clear that it is a real interval, not another instant.

A thing can have two kinds of beginning. One is a boundary of a different kind, such as a point for a line, rest for motion, or an instant for time. The other is its first part, which is of the same kind as the thing itself. A gradual process has no first part of that second kind. No indivisible part can begin a line or stretch of time; even the smallest part that can be imagined can still be divided, and every part has the same nature as the whole.

You may think rest is instantaneous, since it is the absence of motion. But rest is not instantaneous. Motion itself is measured by the moving thing's being between the start and end of its path: at any point on the path, it has not yet reached that point before the instant of arrival, and after arrival it is no longer moving toward it. Rest is measured by two states of the thing in which motion is possible, so it lasts through time. Also, the absence of a gradual process is gradual, as we will see.

Motion in a category requires the thing to have, at every instant, a state in that category different from its state at the instant before and the instant after. That is the test for motion in a category.
That is, gradual in the strict sense of extending across time. The reference is to motion considered as a whole, not to motion through the middle of a path.

The passage names sounds as examples of states that do not remain fixed in themselves but follow from motion. Here the reference is to motion along a straight path and its measures. An angle formed by two crossing lines occurs in an instant; an angle formed by a moving line has no first instant in the same sense as motion itself.
That is, instantaneous things that remain after the first instant in which they exist.
The boundary may come from dividing time in thought or from the different events that occur within it. As explained earlier, time has no boundary in either of the two senses discussed there.

The moving thing is between the start and end of its path in such a way that it has not reached any chosen point just before the instant of reaching it, and is no longer moving toward that point just after.
The flowing now differs both from a single arrival and from one continuous arrival that lasts over time; both of those are temporal in different ways.

The line invites the reader to reflect inwardly. The divine reality is one and simple, though it appears in all things. Differences belong to the things in which it appears, not to God's own presence. If that presence seems to differ from one thing to another, the difference is on the side of the things, not on God's side. God remains; all else passes away.
The issue is how motion ceases after it has existed—its passing away—not the general fact that it is absent at times when it does not exist.

Each imagined part of motion is actual in relation to the part before it, which was its potential, and potential in relation to the part after it, which will become actual. Potential and actual are interwoven in motion. So just as motion comes to exist gradually, it also ceases gradually.

This also means that the natural world, whose existence is always unfolding, does not simply cease at some later time. Its nonexistence, like its coming to be, consists of successive stages. Sadra says in several books that the world's coming to be and its continued existence occupy the same stretch of time. The human soul, too, comes to be over time: its powers and habits are formed by the knowledge it gains from the beginning of life to the end, so it is not complete at a single instant. Its creation includes the whole time in which it exists. The same is true of the greater world. This does not mean that God's act is weak or slow. His command is simply “Be,” and it is. The gradual creation of heaven and earth is what is meant by their being made in six days—the span of the world's life, whose length only God knows. God's gift does not stop or weaken; the whole period unfolds within it. The six days also correspond to the call of the six messengers of resolve. The life of each, including the survival of his teachings and his twelve successors, is described as twelve thousand years: one divine day linked to the manifestation of a thousand of God's names, even if it spans thousands of ordinary years. The sixth day is the age of the Qur'an's revelation, from the first appearance of the Seal of the Prophets and his teachings to the last of his community's spiritual leaders and their rightful rule. Its universal reach and fullness do not cease. The Prophet was a prophet when Adam was still between water and clay, and Abraham was among his followers. His spiritual reality embraced all the intellects, like a universal intellect. Even if this period lasts six days or many thousands of years, to God it is like a glance or less. What is to be will be; the pen has run dry.

This may seem to contradict the earlier claim, from both Sadra and Avicenna, that motion as a whole extends across time, while motion through the middle exists in time without matching it part for part. The apparent conflict can be resolved by considering motion in two ways: its existence is all at once, while its nature is gradual; or motion exists in the world through a changing thing, while motion considered by itself is in the mind. What exists in the mind is not spread across time.

As noted earlier, motion within motion is not impossible; it occurs. What is impossible is an endless chain of changes within changes that never reaches a stable basis. The same applies when one feature belongs to another feature: the chain must end in a substance.
This follows from Sadra's view of substantial motion. Avicenna may have stated something that points toward that view, even if he did not fully adopt it.
This is itself an argument for substantial motion: a substantial form comes to be after another substantial form.
In this second sense, “measure” names a thing by what it causes: the instant makes time countable.
The shared boundary relates equally to both sides. It has no length of its own, so it does not separate them with a gap; it joins them.
This restates the point just made.
“Measure” here means something that makes another thing countable. Motion and time each make the other multiple: motion gives time its earlier and later parts, and time gives motion its count.

People, considered in themselves, have neither continuous nor separate quantity. Their bodies have continuous size, while their number is separate or discrete. The number ten is a quantity that makes them count as ten. Likewise, time is a quantity that measures motion. In this respect, time is to motion as geometrical extension is to a physical body.
Here “measure” means “make something have a certain amount.”
The copies read “by its amount”; the intended meaning is “by showing its amount.” Units of time—such as years, months, weeks, days, hours, and minutes—show how much motion has occurred.
The wording in the copies is unclear. The sense requires “by the amount,” as shown by the examples of the measuring cup and what it contains.

There are not two separate existences here. The path and motion are one existence, considered in different ways. When we consider it through one aspect, it is the cause; through another, it is the effect.
The wording might suggest that motion and its continuity are two separate existences. The distinction exists only in how we think about them.

The word “in” has different meanings in different cases: something can be in a place, in time, in a material, in a subject, or in an essence or existence. So “motion in time,” “time in motion,” “a broader kind in a species,” and “a species in a broader kind” each use “in” in a different way.

The instant is not time, just as unity is not a number; the two are different kinds of things. Earlier and later occur throughout the kinds and parts of time, just as even and odd occur throughout kinds and parts of number. Hours, days, weeks, and months are kinds of time, just as two, three, and four are kinds of number.
The note proposes changing the wording from “two motions flank it” to “two periods of rest flank the motion.”
This does not fit easily with the later claim that other categories change only indirectly through the change of substance. The note leaves that tension for the reader to consider.

The reference is to motion from place to place. As explained earlier, this motion comes before changes in quality and quantity because those depend on it. The circular motion of the outermost sphere is the first and oldest motion of all.

Calling changes in other categories “indirect” conflicts with Sadra's view that they exist as modes of their subject, especially if an accident is a level of the subject's own existence. If the subject changes while its features remain fixed, those features would seem able to exist without it, which is impossible. The better view is that these categories truly change along with substance, not merely by association.

“As they exist” means “in their existence.” Earlier in the book, Sadra says that any being, even a body, belongs to metaphysics simply as something that exists; it belongs to natural philosophy as a body, and to mathematics as something measurable. Still, the timeless duration of changing things is lower than that of purely immaterial beings. The timeless realm, dahr, contains immaterial beings and changing things considered in their luminous aspect. Stable beings, insofar as they depend on the Eternal, belong to the eternal realm, sarmad. God's eternity is beyond any duration—timeless or temporal—and beyond any extension, whether across space or through a chain of things.
Most copies have this wording. It seems to be a copying error: the discussion of motion is marked as a chapter, so it would be strange for some related points to be marked as a stage.

The clearest argument here is that motion begins from pure potentiality. Some people count the actual state at which motion ends as its starting point, but motion ends in pure actuality, without the potential that it contains. Potential and actuality are opposites in this respect. Still, there is no proof that the starting point and destination of every motion are strict opposites. Where they are opposites, that is only by coincidence.
“Larger” and “smaller” here mean the larger and smaller sizes expected within a thing's own kind—not a seed's smallness compared with the size of the outermost sphere.
The two directions are the natural directions. Most motion occurs between them; in reality, there is no single natural motion from one true endpoint all the way to the other.
The beginning and end of circular motion are not points. They are positions, and the two positions are never the same at the same time.

The beginning and end may be found in different, non-overlapping parts of motion. There are also possible beginnings and ends that can coincide because they are relative to what comes before or after. Along with an actual beginning and end, these make three kinds.
This change follows the underlying thing; it is not merely something that happens to it by accident.
